readerTitle: Why the plumber who shows up on time wins
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관공, 청소 서비스, 회계 대행사) + 실제 연구 (Garvin, 1987 품질의 8가지 차원)
insight: 품질은 모든 것을 더 좋게 만드는 일이 아니라, 고객이 중요하게 여기고 알아볼 수 있는 한두 가지 차원을 골라 약속하고 운영 전체를 그 약속에 맞추는 전략적 선택이다.
misconception: 품질은 많을수록 좋고, 모든 면에서 최고가 되면 고객은 저절로 알아본다.

sources.text: Garvin, D. A. (1987). Competing on the Eight Dimensions of Quality. Harvard Business Review.
배관공, 청소 서비스, 회계 대행사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Garvin(1987)의 8가지 차원(performance, features, reliability, conformance, durability, serviceability, aesthetics, perceived quality) 목록과 논문 제목·연도를 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 차원 일부만 소개하고 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
모든 사업 사례(배관공, 청소 서비스, 회계 대행사)는 가상입니다. 수치나 통계를 만들어 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the plumber who shows up on time wins
body: Two plumbers fix the same leak equally well. One arrives sometime between 9 and 5. The other arrives inside a one-hour window, wears shoe covers and texts you a photo of the finished pipe.
Most homeowners would call the second one the better plumber. Yet the actual repair was the same.

image.label: Two plumbers at the same front door, one with a clock and shoe covers
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 같은 현관문 앞에 배관공 두 명. 왼쪽은 시계가 흐릿하고 기다리는 집주인, 오른쪽은 신발 커버를 신고 정시에 도착해 휴대폰으로 사진을 보여주는 배관공. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A cheaper rival is taking your customers.
body: You run a home cleaning service. A new rival charges 15% less. Your cleaning is thorough, but customers mention that a different cleaner shows up each time and arrival times vary.
Where do you put your effort?

options.feedback: You may keep some customers, but you give up margin and now compete only on price, where the cheapest player usually wins.

options.text: Upgrade everything: premium products, more tasks per visit, deeper cleans
options.feedback: Better cleaning is real quality, but it raises costs and doesn't touch the complaints customers actually made.

options.text: Promise the same cleaner every visit, on time, with a free redo if anything is missed
options.feedback: This targets what customers notice and care about. It costs scheduling effort, but it gives people a clear reason to pay more than the rival.

cards.title: People rate what they can see.
body: Most customers can't judge how well a floor was disinfected. They can judge whether the same friendly person came, whether she was on time and whether anything was missed.

So in a service business, much of what customers call quality lives in reliability, consistency and how problems get fixed. A firm that wins there can charge more, even if its cleaning is no deeper than anyone else's.

cards.title: Quality as strategy
body: **Quality as strategy** means choosing which kinds of quality you will compete on, then making them a promise customers can count on.

Harvard professor David Garvin argued in 1987 that quality has several separate dimensions, such as performance, reliability, durability, serviceability and how well a product matches its promise. A business rarely leads on all of them. It picks the few its customers value most.

image.label: Quality split into several dials, two turned up high
image.brief: 계기판 인포그래픽. 다이얼 6개에 "Performance", "Reliability", "Durability", "Serviceability", "Features", "Looks" 라벨. 그중 "Reliability"와 "Serviceability" 두 개만 최대로 올라가 있고 나머지는 중간.

cards.title: Choose, promise, then build around it.
body: Turning quality into strategy usually takes three steps:
list: **Choose** the one or two dimensions your customers notice and care about most
**Promise** them out loud, ideally with a guarantee
**Build** hiring, scheduling, training and pricing so the promise holds every time
cards.callout: A promise you keep 95% of the time is a weaker strategy than a smaller promise you keep every time.
cards.softwareNote: A software company might choose reliability over features: fewer releases, strong uptime and fast support replies. That choice then shapes how it tests code, staffs support and prices plans.

cards.title: Cheap can be high quality too.
body: Quality doesn't mean luxury. A budget motel can be high quality if every room is clean, the bed is comfortable and the price on the sign is the price you pay. It simply chose different dimensions than a five-star hotel.
The mistake is the middle ground: trying to be a bit better at everything. Costs rise, yet customers can't name one thing you do best.

cards.title: Quality only pays if customers value it.
body: Extra quality that customers don't notice or won't pay for is just cost. Ask or watch them before you invest.
Choosing also means accepting trade-offs. The cleaning firm that guarantees the same cleaner may be less flexible on last-minute bookings.
And a broken promise hurts more than no promise. If you advertise on-time arrival, one late visit stings more than it would for a rival who promised nothing.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You run a bookkeeping service for small businesses. Your accuracy is good, as is everyone's. Clients say their biggest worry is not knowing where their numbers stand, and slow replies when tax deadlines loom.

options.text: Guarantee monthly books closed by day 5 and replies within one business day
options.feedback: This targets the worries clients named and is easy for them to see. It requires tighter workflows and staffing near deadlines.

options.text: Add more reports and dashboards to every package
options.feedback: More features can help, but they don't fix late numbers or slow replies, and they add work for your team.

options.text: Hire senior accountants to push accuracy even higher
options.feedback: Accuracy matters, but clients already see it as standard. You'd raise costs on a dimension they can't tell apart.

cards.title: Pick the quality your customers notice, and never miss it.
body: Quality becomes strategy when you choose a few dimensions, promise them and build your operations so the promise always holds.
**Try it today:** ask three customers why they chose you. Circle the quality they mention most. Is it something you promise openly, and keep every time?
